```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
    collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5

```

# About this tutorial

A **hit** is a gene whose barcodes change consistently in the treated samples
compared with the control samples. In a dropout (loss of function) screen the
interesting hits are usually depleted: their knockdown kills the cells only in
the presence of the treatment.

This tutorial goes through the functions of ScreenR that find hits and check
them, one step at a time:

1. tell ScreenR which samples to compare (design matrix and contrasts);
2. test each gene with FRY, ROAST and CAMERA;
3. test each gene with the Z-score methods;
4. compare the methods and combine their results;
5. use several time points;
6. check the candidates in the data, barcode by barcode.

It uses the example screen of ScreenR. The complete analysis of this screen,
from the quality control to the list of the genes to validate, is in the
[longitudinal screen vignette](Longitudinal_Screen_Analysis.html); here the
focus is on how each function works and how to read its result.

# The data

```{r packages, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(ScreenR)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

The plots of ScreenR have no theme of their own: choose one for the whole
session with `theme_set()`.

```{r theme}
theme_set(theme_light(base_size = 12))
```

The screen has two samples taken before the treatment (`Time1`, before the
infection, and `Time2`, after the puromycin selection), then three treated
(`TRT`) and three control (`CTRL`) replicates 7 days (`Time3`) and 14 days
(`Time4`) after the selection. The `sample_table` describes the samples, the
`groups` (used by the statistical models) are the combinations of time point
and treatment, and the `palettes` give each value of the sample variables the
same color in every plot.

```{r object, message=FALSE}
data(count_table)
data(annotation_table)

samples <- data.frame(
    Sample = c("Time1", "Time2",
        paste0("Time3_TRT_", c("A", "B", "C")),
        paste0("Time3_CTRL_", c("A", "B", "C")),
        paste0("Time4_TRT_", c("A", "B", "C")),
        paste0("Time4_CTRL_", c("A", "B", "C"))),
    Day = c("Time1", "Time2", rep(c("Time3", "Time4"), each = 6)),
    Treatment = c("Time1", "Time2", rep(rep(c("TRT", "CTRL"), each = 3), 2))
)
groups <- factor(ifelse(samples$Day %in% c("Time1", "Time2"), "T1/T2",
    paste(samples$Day, samples$Treatment, sep = "_")))

counts <- filter(count_table, Barcode != "*")
colnames(counts) <- c("Barcode", samples$Sample)

object <- create_screenr_object(
    table = counts, annotation = annotation_table, groups = groups,
    sample_table = samples,
    palettes = list(
        Treatment = c(Time1 = "#CCCCCC", Time2 = "#999999",
            CTRL = "#1B9E77", TRT = "#D95F02"),
        Day = c(Time1 = "#CCCCCC", Time2 = "#999999",
            Time3 = "#7570B3", Time4 = "#E7298A"),
        Group = c(`T1/T2` = "#999999", Time3_CTRL = "#66C2A5",
            Time3_TRT = "#FC8D62", Time4_CTRL = "#1B9E77",
            Time4_TRT = "#D95F02")
    )
)
object <- remove_all_zero_row(object)
get_sample_table(object)
```

The counts are normalized once, and the same normalization is used by every
function below: the hit-finding methods, the fold changes and the plots.
TMM is used here, as in the longitudinal vignette (see `?normalize_data` for
the methods and for when TMM is biased).

```{r normalize}
object <- normalize_data(object, method = "tmm")
get_normalization(object)$method
```

# Overview of the methods

| Method | Function | What it tests | Reference | Uses replicates |
|--------|----------|---------------|-----------|-----------------|
| FRY | `find_roast_hit(method = "fry")` | The barcodes of the gene change | None (self-contained) | Yes |
| ROAST | `find_roast_hit()` | As FRY, with random rotations | None (self-contained) | Yes |
| CAMERA | `find_camera_hit()` | The barcodes of the gene change more than the others | The other genes (competitive) | Yes |
| Gene-level Z-score | `find_gene_zscore_hit()` | The mean Z-score of the barcodes of the gene is extreme | Random sets of barcodes, or the empirical null | With `compute_barcode_statistics()` |
| All time points | `find_consistent_hit()` | The gene changes at every time point | As the chosen method | Yes |
| Time course | `find_time_hit()` | The treatment effect changes over time | None | Yes |
| Legacy Z-score rules | `find_zscore_hit()`, `find_robust_zscore_hit()` | Counts barcodes below the median Z-score | None | No |

The **FDR** (false discovery rate) is the expected proportion of false hits
among the genes you call hits: with an FDR cut off of 5%, about 1 in 20 of the
reported genes is expected to be a false positive. Each method returns only the
genes with `FDR <= fdr` (default 0.05); use `fdr = 1` to get all the genes and
rank them yourself, as done below.

# Step 1: which samples to compare

The methods that use the replicates fit a linear model, which needs two
things:

* a **design matrix**, which says which group each sample belongs to;
* a **contrast**, which says which groups to compare.

`create_design_matrix()` builds the design matrix from the groups of the
object: one column per group, and a 1 in the column of the group of each
sample. Group names that are not valid R names are changed (`T1/T2` becomes
`T1.T2`).

```{r design}
design <- create_design_matrix(object)
design
```

`create_contrast()` builds the comparison between groups by name: here
treated against control at each time point.

```{r contrasts}
contrast_time3 <- create_contrast(design,
    treatment = "Time3_TRT", control = "Time3_CTRL"
)
contrast_time4 <- create_contrast(design,
    treatment = "Time4_TRT", control = "Time4_CTRL"
)
contrast_time4
```

The contrast gives +1 to the treated group and -1 to the control group: the
result is the treated minus the control. With several groups on one side
(for example `treatment = c("Time3_TRT", "Time4_TRT")`) their average is used.

**Common mistake.** Do not build the design with `model.matrix(~ groups)` and
rename its columns: the first group becomes the intercept and the columns are
in alphabetical order, so the names end up on the wrong columns and the wrong
samples are compared. `create_design_matrix()` and `create_contrast()` avoid
this, and every function that takes a design checks that its rows are the
samples of the object, in the same order.

The examples below compare treated and control samples at Time4, the time
point with the larger effect.

# Step 2: FRY, ROAST and CAMERA

These methods test the barcodes of each gene as a set, with edgeR on the raw
counts and the normalization of the object.

* **FRY and ROAST** ask whether the barcodes of a gene **change at all** (a
  self-contained test). ROAST uses random rotations: set `seed` to get the
  same result every time and use many rotations (`nrot`, default 9999) for a
  real analysis; here 999 keep the tutorial fast. FRY (`method = "fry"`)
  computes the same test exactly, without rotations: it is faster, its
  p-values are not limited by the number of rotations, and it is the
  recommended choice.
* **CAMERA** asks whether the barcodes of a gene change **more than the other
  barcodes** (a competitive test), taking into account the correlation between
  barcodes.

The two kinds of tests answer different questions. A self-contained test
calls a gene when its barcodes are depleted more than the replicates vary,
even if many genes are depleted; a competitive test calls it only when it
stands out from the rest of the library, so it becomes conservative when many
genes have an effect. On the other hand FRY and ROAST rely on the variability
between replicates: they need replicates in both groups, have little power
with two replicates or noisy data, and find almost nothing when the control is
a single sample (for example a plasmid library). All the p-values are
one-sided, for the requested direction.

`number_barcode` sets the minimum number of barcodes (more than
`number_barcode`) a gene needs to be tested, and `direction` chooses depleted
(`"Down"`) or enriched (`"Up"`) genes.

```{r fry-roast-camera}
fry <- find_roast_hit(object, design, contrast_time4,
    method = "fry", fdr = 1
)
head(fry)

roast <- find_roast_hit(object, design, contrast_time4,
    nrot = 999, seed = 42, fdr = 1
)
camera <- find_camera_hit(object, design, contrast_time4, fdr = 1)
head(camera)
```

| Column | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `NGenes` | Number of barcodes of the gene |
| `Direction` | Down or Up |
| `PValue`, `FDR` | Significance for the requested direction |
| `PValue.Mixed`, `FDR.Mixed` (FRY, ROAST) | Significance of a change in either direction of the barcodes |
| `PropDown`, `PropUp` (ROAST) | Proportion of barcodes going down or up |
| `Log2FC` | Median log2 fold change of the barcodes |

Use `PValue` and `FDR`: the "Mixed" columns test whether the barcodes change
in any direction, so they also call genes whose barcodes disagree.

# Step 3: the Z-score methods

## Fold changes and Z-scores

`compute_metrics()` averages the replicates of the treated and of the control
samples of one time point and computes for each barcode:

| Column | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `Treated`, `Control` | Mean normalized count |
| `Log2FC` | log2((Treated + 0.5) / (Control + 0.5)): negative means depleted in the treated samples |
| `Zscore` | Log2FC standardized with the mean and standard deviation of all barcodes |
| `ZscoreRobust` | Log2FC standardized with the median and MAD, less sensitive to outliers |

The `treatment` and `control` arguments are values of the Treatment column of
`get_sample_table()`, and `day` a value of its Day column.

```{r metrics}
metrics_time3 <- compute_metrics(object,
    control = "CTRL", treatment = "TRT", day = "Time3"
)
metrics_time4 <- compute_metrics(object,
    control = "CTRL", treatment = "TRT", day = "Time4"
)
head(metrics_time4)
```

`plot_zscore_distribution()` compares the Z-scores of several time points: a
treatment with an effect gives a longer left tail at the later time point. It
receives the tables, not the object, so the palette of the time points is
given explicitly to keep the colors of the other plots:

```{r zscore-distribution}
plot_zscore_distribution(
    list(Time3 = metrics_time3, Time4 = metrics_time4),
    alpha = 0.6, palette = get_palettes(object)$Day
)
```

## Using the replicates

`compute_metrics()` averages the replicates, so it cannot tell a consistent
barcode from a noisy one. `compute_barcode_statistics()` tests each barcode
with edgeR, using the variability between replicates, and returns a Z-score
with the same columns. This is the recommended input of the gene-level test.

```{r barcode-statistics}
barcode_statistics <- compute_barcode_statistics(
    object, design, contrast_time4
)
head(barcode_statistics)
```

## Gene-level test

`find_gene_zscore_hit()` computes for each gene the mean Z-score of its
barcodes (`statistic = "median"` uses the median, which is less affected by a
single barcode with a strong, possibly off-target, effect) and compares it
with a reference distribution:

* `reference = "random"` (default): the scores of random sets of barcodes of
  the same size, drawn `n_permutations` times (`seed` makes it
  reproducible). With `control_genes` the random sets are drawn from control
  genes instead. Do this only if the controls behave like genes without
  effect: non-targeting shRNAs often do not (targeting shRNAs are usually
  somewhat depleted compared with them, so every gene looks depleted).
* `reference = "empirical"`: the distribution of the scores of the genes
  without effect, estimated from the centre of the distribution of all the
  genes. It accounts for the barcodes of a gene varying together, which makes
  the random sets give too small p-values, especially in shRNA screens. It
  needs a library with hundreds of genes, most of them without effect (see
  the [empirical null vignette](Empirical_null.html)).

```{r gene-zscore}
zscore <- find_gene_zscore_hit(barcode_statistics, fdr = 1, seed = 1)
zscore_empirical <- find_gene_zscore_hit(barcode_statistics,
    reference = "empirical", fdr = 1
)
head(zscore_empirical)
```

| Column | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `NBarcodes` | Number of barcodes of the gene |
| `Score` | Mean Z-score of the barcodes |
| `Log2FC` | Median log2 fold change of the barcodes |
| `PValue`, `FDR` | Significance |

`plot_empirical_null()` shows the gene scores and the fitted null, which
should follow the centre of the distribution:

```{r empirical-null, fig.height = 3.5}
plot_empirical_null(barcode_statistics)
```

Here the null is almost the standard normal (mean
`r round(attr(zscore_empirical, "null")["mean"], 2)`, standard deviation
`r round(attr(zscore_empirical, "null")["sd"], 2)`), with no long tail of
depleted genes: the treatment effect is moderate and concerns a few genes.

## Legacy rules

`find_zscore_hit()` and `find_robust_zscore_hit()` call a gene a hit when more
than `number_barcode` of its barcodes are below the median Z-score. They are
kept for compatibility, but they do not give a p-value and many genes without
an effect pass them by chance (about 17% with 10 barcodes and
`number_barcode = 6`): prefer `find_gene_zscore_hit()`.

```{r legacy}
nrow(find_zscore_hit(metrics_time4, number_barcode = 6))
```

# Step 4: comparing and combining the methods

## How many genes each method finds

```{r fdr-levels}
results <- list(
    FRY = fry, ROAST = roast, CAMERA = camera,
    `Z-score` = zscore, `Z-score (empirical)` = zscore_empirical
)
fdr_levels <- c(0.05, 0.1, 0.25)
bind_rows(lapply(results, function(result) {
    vapply(fdr_levels, function(x) sum(result$FDR <= x), integer(1))
}), .id = "Method") %>%
    mutate(FDR = paste0(100 * fdr_levels, "%"), .before = 1)
```

FRY, the most powerful test here, finds `r sum(fry$FDR <= 0.05)` genes at 5%
FDR. ROAST tests the same hypothesis, but with 999 rotations its p-values
cannot be smaller than 1/1000, which after the correction for the
`r nrow(roast)` genes is not enough to reach 5% (use `nrot = 9999`, or FRY).
The competitive tests (CAMERA and the Z-score tests) find none at 5%: the
depletions are reproducible, but they do not stand out against all the other
genes of the library. Choose the cut off before looking at the results and
report it; below, 10% is used to compare the methods.

## Overlap between the methods

`plot_common_hit()` takes the results of any number of methods (any table
with Gene and FDR) and shows the overlap of their hits at the cut off given
with `fdr`. With up to three methods it draws a Venn diagram:

```{r venn, fig.height = 5}
plot_common_hit(results[c("FRY", "ROAST", "CAMERA")], fdr = 0.1,
    title = "Depleted genes at Time4 (10% FDR)")
```

With more methods it draws an UpSet plot: each column is a combination of
methods (the dots below), and the bar on top counts the genes found by exactly
that combination; the bars on the left count the genes found by each method.

```{r upset, fig.height = 4.5, fig.width = 8}
plot_common_hit(results, fdr = 0.1,
    title = "Depleted genes at Time4 (10% FDR)")
```

`find_common_hit()` returns the genes found by at least `common_in` methods
(by default by all of them):

```{r common}
common <- find_common_hit(results, fdr = 0.1, common_in = 3)
common
```

`summarise_hits()` puts the FDR of every method in one table. `NMethods`
counts the methods in which the gene passes the cut off, and `MaxFDR` (the
largest FDR) is a conservative score to rank the genes supported by all the
methods. Pass the tables computed with `fdr = 1`, so that every gene has a
value.

```{r summary}
summary <- summarise_hits(results, fdr = 0.1)
summary %>%
    select(Gene, starts_with("FDR"), NMethods) %>%
    head(8) %>%
    knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

`plot_volcano()` shows every gene with its effect (x) and its significance
(y): the hits are above the dashed line, and the most significant are
labelled. Here the 12 genes that FRY finds at 10% FDR:

```{r volcano, fig.height = 4.5}
plot_volcano(fry, fdr = 0.1)
```

With the table of `summarise_hits()` the significance is the largest FDR of
the methods, so the genes above the line are found by every method; give the
barcode statistics, from which the mean log2 fold change of each gene is
computed: `plot_volcano(summary, statistics = barcode_statistics)`. None of
the genes of this screen is found by all five methods at 10% FDR.

The combined list has no guaranteed false discovery rate: treat it as a short
list of candidates to check and validate.

# Step 5: several time points

"Depleted over time" can mean different things, which need different tests.

## Depleted at every time point

`find_consistent_hit()` runs the same method for several contrasts and calls
a gene only if it is depleted in **all** of them (an intersection-union test:
the p-value of the gene is the largest of its p-values, then corrected for the
number of genes).

```{r consistent}
consistent <- find_consistent_hit(object, design,
    contrasts = list(Time3 = contrast_time3, Time4 = contrast_time4),
    method = "fry", fdr = 1
)
head(consistent)
```

The smallest FDR is `r signif(min(consistent$FDR), 2)`: no gene is depleted at
both time points. The candidates of Time4 have small effects at Time3 (see
`Log2FC_Time3`), so in this screen the treatment-specific depletion appears
at the later time point. `combine_consistent_hits()` does the same with
tables of p-values computed beforehand.

## A treatment effect that changes over time

`find_time_hit()` asks whether the treatment effect **changes over time**,
with one model for the treated and control samples of all the time points:
untreated and treated samples each follow a line over time, and the method
tests the difference between the slopes. Give the real times of the time
points with `time` (here days after the selection); otherwise they are
treated as equally spaced. Samples taken before the treatment can be added as
untreated samples with `baseline`, when their times are known too.

```{r time}
time_hit <- find_time_hit(object,
    treatment = "TRT", control = "CTRL",
    days = c("Time3", "Time4"), time = c(Time3 = 7, Time4 = 14),
    fdr = 1
)
head(time_hit)
```

`Log2FC` is the change of the treatment log2 fold change per day: a negative
value means that the depletion grows over time. With two time points this is
the difference between the effects at Time4 and at Time3, divided by 7 days.
Here `r sum(time_hit$FDR <= 0.05)` genes have an FDR below 5% (smallest FDR
`r signif(min(time_hit$FDR), 2)`): the effects grow between the two time
points, but not enough to be detected gene by gene with three replicates.

# Step 6: checking the candidates

Statistics can produce false positives, so look at the data of each
candidate. The candidates here are the genes found by at least three of the
five methods at 10% FDR:

```{r candidates}
candidates <- common
candidates
```

## Trend over time

`plot_trend()` shows the mean normalized count of the barcodes of a gene in
each sample over the time points. With `color_by` the treated and control
samples get their own trend (the mean of each time point), the samples before
the treatment are drawn once as shared references (`reference_groups`), and
`highlight_difference` shades the gap between the two conditions. A
treatment-specific hit goes down in the treated samples more than in the
controls.

```{r trend, fig.height = 4, fig.width = 9}
plot_trend(object,
    genes = candidates, group_var = c("Time1", "Time2", "CTRL", "TRT"),
    color_by = "Treatment", reference_groups = c("Time1", "Time2"),
    connect_reference = TRUE, highlight_difference = TRUE,
    nrow = 1, scales = "free_y"
) +
    labs(x = "Time point (equally spaced)",
        y = "Mean normalized counts per shRNA")
```

## Size of the effect

`plot_treatment_separation()` shows the log2 ratio of the treated to the
control samples at each time point, labelled with the percentage difference.
It shows how far the conditions separate and at which time point; it is
descriptive, not a test.

Gene_173 and Gene_422 decrease in the treated samples while the controls
stay stable or grow. Gene_296 decreases in the controls too (its knockdown
slows growth even without the treatment), and more in the treated samples:
the treatment adds to a fitness effect.

```{r separation, fig.height = 3.5, fig.width = 9}
plot_treatment_separation(object, candidates,
    treatment = "TRT", control = "CTRL", nrow = 1
)
```

## Distribution of the barcodes

`plot_boxplot()` shows the normalized counts of all the barcodes of a gene in
each sample, colored by the variable given with `fill_var` (here with the
palette of the Treatment):

```{r boxplot, fig.height = 4}
plot_boxplot(object,
    genes = candidates[1], group_var = c("TRT", "CTRL"),
    fill_var = "Treatment"
) +
    scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis(angle = 45))
```

## Barcode by barcode

A real hit should be supported by most of its barcodes, not by one or two.
`plot_barcode_heatmap()` shows every barcode of the genes in every sample,
centred on the mean of the barcode across the samples shown: blue is lower and
red higher than the usual abundance of the barcode.

```{r heatmap, fig.height = 6, fig.width = 9}
plot_barcode_heatmap(object, candidates, column_group = "Day") +
    scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis(angle = 60))
```

At Time4 several barcodes of each gene are lower in the treated samples than
in the controls, so the depletion is not driven by a single barcode; it is
clearest for Gene_296. The effects are moderate, and they vary between the
replicates.

`plot_barcode_trend()` shows the log2 fold change of each barcode at each time
point (it returns one plot per gene):

```{r barcode-trend, fig.height = 4}
barcode_trends <- plot_barcode_trend(
    list(Time3 = metrics_time3, Time4 = metrics_time4),
    genes = candidates[1]
)
barcode_trends[[candidates[1]]]
```

`plot_barcode_hit()` ranks all the barcodes by their log2 fold change and
places the barcodes of a gene on the ranking (vertical lines): most lines on
the left side means that the gene is depleted. The line on top shows where
the barcodes of the gene are concentrated (above 1, dashed line), and the
bottom panel shows their log2 fold changes (`show_log2fc = FALSE` hides it):

```{r barcode-hit, fig.height = 5}
plot_barcode_hit(object, design,
    contrast = contrast_time4, gene = candidates[1]
)
```

`find_discordant_barcodes()` lists the barcodes that behave very differently
from the other barcodes of their gene, which may have off-target effects.
They are a warning to read the result of the gene with care; do not remove
them before the tests.

```{r discordant}
discordant <- find_discordant_barcodes(metrics_time4, threshold = 3)
filter(discordant, Gene %in% candidates)
```

## Additional filters

Two filters can remove candidates that are not convincing:

* `filter_by_slope()` keeps the genes whose normalized counts decrease more
  over time in the treated samples than in the control samples (with `time`,
  the slopes are per unit of time);
* `filter_by_variance()` removes the genes whose barcodes disagree too much
  (variance of the barcode log2 fold changes above `variance`).

```{r filters}
filter_by_slope(object,
    genes = candidates,
    group_var_treatment = "TRT", group_var_control = "CTRL",
    time = c(Time3 = 7, Time4 = 14)
)

filter_by_variance(object,
    genes = candidates, matrix_model = design,
    contrast = contrast_time4, variance = 0.5
) %>%
    distinct(Gene, Variance)
```

# Summary

| Step | What to do |
|------|------------|
| 1 | `create_design_matrix()` and `create_contrast()` for the comparison |
| 2 | `find_roast_hit(method = "fry")`; `find_camera_hit()` for a competitive test |
| 3 | `compute_barcode_statistics()` + `find_gene_zscore_hit()`, with `reference = "empirical"` for shRNA libraries |
| 4 | `plot_common_hit()`, `find_common_hit()`, `summarise_hits()` and `plot_volcano()` |
| 5 | `find_consistent_hit()` (every time point) and `find_time_hit()` (an effect that changes over time) |
| 6 | `plot_trend()`, `plot_treatment_separation()`, `plot_boxplot()`, `plot_barcode_heatmap()`, `plot_barcode_hit()`, `find_discordant_barcodes()` |

Choose the FDR cut off before the analysis, report it, and validate the
candidates experimentally. The
[longitudinal screen vignette](Longitudinal_Screen_Analysis.html) puts these
steps together and ends with the genes of this screen to validate.

```{r session}
sessionInfo()
```
